assert abs(kyles_lambda(y, x) - np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]) < 1e-12
try:
    kyles_lambda([1.0, 2.0], [5.0, 5.0])
    raise SystemExit("flat flow should fail")
except ValueError:
    pass

name: Probability of Informed Trading (PIN)
summary: The share of trading that the Easley-Kiefer-O'Hara-Paperman model attributes to informed traders, given the chance of an information event and the arrival rates of informed and uninformed orders.
definition: PIN is the model's probability that the next trade comes from an informed trader. An information event occurs with probability α. If it does, informed orders arrive at rate μ, on the buy side or the sell side according to the news. Uninformed buys and sells arrive at rates ε_b and ε_s whether or not there was news. PIN is the expected informed arrival divided by the expected total arrival. Estimating α, μ and the epsilons is a separate maximum-likelihood problem on daily buy and sell counts. This page evaluates the formula once those parameters are in hand. It does not fit them.
formula:
PIN = α μ / (α μ + ε_b + ε_s)

α   probability of an information event, in [0, 1]
μ   arrival rate of informed traders when there is news
ε_b, ε_s  arrival rates of uninformed buyers and sellers

The denominator is the expected rate of all trades.
PIN is between 0 and 1 when the inputs are valid.

sections.heading: What you do with the parameters
sections.html:
• Once a fit exists, PIN summarises it in one number. Comparing PIN across names is comparing those fits, so the count data, the day length and the optimiser have to be the same kind of exercise.
  • The high-frequency imbalance that is often used in place of a daily fit is VPIN. It does not estimate α and μ.
  • A price-impact slope is a different object again: Kyle's lambda.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The formula is not the estimator. The likelihood is a mixture of Poissons and it has well known local maxima, including the buy-sell symmetry of the original model. A closed form for PIN does not remove that. This function will happily turn a bad fit into a precise-looking ratio.
  • Buys and sells must be classified first. The classic papers use a trade-classification algorithm. Different signs, different PIN.
  • Zero total intensity. If every rate is zero the ratio is undefined. The function raises.

faq.question: Why doesn't this page estimate PIN?
faq.answer: The estimate is a constrained maximum-likelihood fit of a Poisson mixture, and the likelihood is not concave. A short optimiser pasted into a glossary page would look authoritative and land in local maxima. The page publishes the map from parameters to PIN, which is the part with a closed form.

faq.question: What does a PIN of 0.2 mean?
faq.answer: Inside the model, one trade in five is from an informed trader, at the estimated arrival rates. Outside the model it is only as meaningful as the fit. It is not a probability you can read off the tape without estimating the parameters.

test:
assert abs(pin(0.4, 50, 20, 30) - 20 / 70) < 1e-15
assert pin(0, 100, 10, 10) == 0
assert abs(pin(1, 5, 0, 0) - 1) < 1e-15
try:
    pin(1.2, 1, 1, 1)
    raise SystemExit("alpha above 1 should fail")
except ValueError:
    pass

name: Sharpe Ratio
summary: Mean excess return divided by the standard deviation of excess return, annualised by the square root of the number of periods per year. The same definition as the performance calculator on this site.
definition: The Sharpe ratio asks how much excess return a series delivered per unit of volatility. Excess is the periodic return minus a periodic risk-free rate. The rate used here is an annual rate converted by compound interest, (1 + r_f)^(1/P) − 1, not a simple r_f/P. Volatility is the sample standard deviation (divide by n − 1). Annualisation multiplies by sqrt(P). A higher number means more excess return per unit of variability in that sample. It is not a forecast and it is not a certificate of skill.
formula:
r_f,period = (1 + r_f,annual) ^ (1/P) − 1
excess_t   = R_t − r_f,period

Sharpe = mean(excess) / std(excess, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

P = 252 by default, 242 for China A-shares, 365 for a crypto-style calendar.
std = 0 → the ratio is undefined (returned as NaN).

sections.heading: Conventions that change the number
sections.html:
• The performance calculator uses this compounding convention, sample standard deviation, and the same sqrt(P) annualisation. The glossary function is written to match it.
  • Some published Sharpes subtract r_f/P, or divide by the population standard deviation, or leave the ratio un-annualised. Those are different statistics. Quote P and the risk-free treatment next to the number.
  • Downside-only volatility is the Sortino ratio. Active return over tracking error is the information ratio.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• It is a sample moment. A short window, or a window that happens to contain one regime, moves the ratio a lot. It does not carry a promise about the next window.
  • Volatility is not the risk you may care about. Two series with the same Sharpe can have very different drawdowns and tail losses. See also VaR and expected shortfall.
  • Illiquid and smoothed returns look better. A series that only updates occasionally understates standard deviation and overstates Sharpe. The same is true of a backtest that ignores costs.
  • Annualising assumes i.i.d. periods. Strong autocorrelation makes sqrt(P) the wrong scaling. The function still multiplies by sqrt(P); the assumption is yours to check.

faq.question: Why compound the risk-free rate instead of dividing by 252?
faq.answer: An annual rate of 2 percent is not 2/252 per day under compound interest. The per-period rate that compounds back to 2 percent is (1.02)^(1/252) − 1, which is slightly less than 2/252. The difference is small at low rates and is the convention the performance calculator on this site uses.

faq.question: Is a Sharpe ratio of 1 good?
faq.answer: It means the sample's mean excess return equalled its annualised volatility. Whether that is attractive depends on the sample, the costs that were left out, and the drawdowns. The ratio is not a threshold for taking a position.

test:
import numpy as np
r = np.array([0.01, 0.03])
assert abs(sharpe_ratio(r) - 0.02 / np.sqrt(0.0002) * np.sqrt(252)) < 1e-12
rf = (1.02) ** (1 / 252) - 1
ex = r - rf
assert abs(sharpe_ratio(r, rf_annual=0.02) - ex.mean() / ex.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)) < 1e-12
assert np.isnan(sharpe_ratio([0.01, 0.01]))
assert sharpe_ratio([0.0, 0.0]) != sharpe_ratio([0.0, 0.0]) or np.isnan(sharpe_ratio([0.0, 0.0]))

name: Sortino Ratio
summary: Mean return above a minimum acceptable return, divided by downside deviation and annualised. Upside variation does not enter the denominator.
definition: The Sortino ratio replaces the Sharpe denominator with downside deviation: the root-mean-square of returns that fall short of a target, with shortfalls of zero on periods that meet the target still included in the average. The target used here is an annual minimum acceptable return, converted to a per-period rate the same way the risk-free rate is converted for the Sharpe ratio. The result is annualised by sqrt(P). It penalises missing the target. It does not penalise beating it.
formula:
MAR_period = (1 + MAR_annual) ^ (1/P) − 1
d_t = min(R_t − MAR_period, 0)
DD  = sqrt( mean(d_t²) )                 average over every period, not only the negative ones

Sortino = (mean(R) − MAR_period) / DD · sqrt(P)

DD = 0 → undefined (NaN). Using only the negative periods in the mean would be a different statistic.

sections.heading: Why the denominator ignores upside
sections.html:
• Two strategies can share a volatility and a Sharpe ratio while one of them makes its volatility on the upside. Sortino treats those as different.
  • The target is not automatically the risk-free rate. It is whatever minimum acceptable return you pass in. Zero means "negative periodic returns count against the strategy".
  • The performance calculator uses this downside definition (root-mean-square over all periods) and the same annualisation.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• A sample with no down period is undefined, not infinite. The function returns NaN. Reporting a huge Sortino from a handful of up days is a presentation choice the code refuses.
  • The mean in the square root is over n, not n − 1. That matches the calculator. Mixing it with a sample-standard-deviation downside changes the number.
  • It still does not see path. A slow grind below the target and a crash with the same squared shortfalls can share a Sortino. Look at maximum drawdown as well.

faq.question: Why average the squared shortfalls over periods that were not shortfalls?
faq.answer: Those periods contribute a zero, so they dilute the root-mean-square. Dropping them would divide by the number of bad periods only and would make a rare crash look like a small downside. The version that keeps the zeros is the one the performance calculator uses.

faq.question: Should the target be the risk-free rate?
faq.answer: Only if that is the return you have decided is the minimum you care about. The parameter is a minimum acceptable return, not a funding rate. Leaving it at zero scores any negative periodic return as downside.

test:
import numpy as np
r = np.array([0.02, -0.01, 0.0])
dd = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.minimum(r, 0.0) ** 2))
assert abs(sortino_ratio(r) - (r.mean() / dd * np.sqrt(252))) < 1e-12
assert np.isnan(sortino_ratio([0.01, 0.02]))

name: Information Ratio
summary: Mean active return versus a benchmark, divided by the tracking error of that active return, and annualised. It scores how large and how steady the gap versus the benchmark was.
definition: Active return is the portfolio's periodic return minus the benchmark's periodic return over the same periods. The information ratio is the mean of that difference divided by its sample standard deviation, multiplied by sqrt(P). It is the Sharpe ratio of the active returns, with the benchmark playing the role of the risk-free asset and no extra cash rate. A positive ratio means the portfolio's sample average was above the benchmark. It does not say the average will stay there.
formula:
a_t = R_port,t − R_bench,t
IR  = mean(a) / std(a, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

Tracking error is the denominator before dividing into the mean: TE = std(a) · sqrt(P).
IR = mean(a) · sqrt(P) / TE, with TE in annualised units.
std(a) = 0 → NaN (the portfolio matched the benchmark exactly in-sample).

sections.heading: Relation to other ratios
sections.html:
• Tracking error is the annualised standard deviation alone. The information ratio puts the mean active return on top of it.
  • The information coefficient is a cross-sectional correlation between a signal and later returns, not this time-series ratio. Grinold's approximation IR ≈ IC · sqrt(breadth) is a model that links them, not an identity in the data.
  • A Sharpe ratio uses excess return over cash. An information ratio uses excess return over the benchmark you were hired to beat, or chose to compare with.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The benchmark has to be the one that was investable on that timing. Comparing a close-to-close portfolio with a benchmark that includes a return the portfolio could not have earned inflates the ratio.
  • Alignment. Missing dates, dividends in one series only, or a different currency, all land in the active return. The function subtracts the two arrays as given.
  • A high IR on a tiny active risk can be a few basis points of average difference and a tracking error that is mostly noise. Report the tracking error beside the ratio.

faq.question: How is this different from the information coefficient?
faq.answer: The information coefficient correlates a cross-section of forecasts with a cross-section of outcomes on one date. The information ratio divides a time series of active returns by their standard deviation. Similar names, different objects.

faq.question: Should the active return include fees?
faq.answer: If the question is what the investor kept versus the benchmark, yes. If the question is whether the holdings differed from the benchmark before costs, no. The function uses the two return series you pass in, so the choice of fees happens before the call.

test:
import numpy as np
port = np.array([0.02, 0.00, 0.01, -0.01])
bench = np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.00, -0.02])
a = port - bench
assert abs(information_ratio(port, bench) - a.mean() / a.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)) < 1e-12
assert np.isnan(information_ratio(bench, bench))

name: Tracking Error
summary: The annualised sample standard deviation of portfolio return minus benchmark return. It measures how far the two series wandered from each other, not whether one ended ahead.
definition: Tracking error is the volatility of active returns. A portfolio that beats its benchmark by exactly one basis point every period has a positive average active return and a tracking error of zero. A portfolio that oscillates around the benchmark has tracking error and, possibly, a zero average. The implementation is the sample standard deviation of the paired difference, times sqrt(P).
formula:
a_t = R_port,t − R_bench,t
TE  = std(a, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

P defaults to 252. Reported as a decimal (0.02 means 2 percent annualised), not in basis points.
The information ratio is mean(a) / std(a) · sqrt(P), so IR = annualised mean active return / TE.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
sections.html:
• Index tracking and closet indexing. A mandate that says "stay within 2 percent tracking error" is a constraint on this number, usually estimated on an ex-ante covariance as well as measured ex post. This function is the ex-post measurement.
  • Next to the information ratio, which is undefined when tracking error is zero.
  • Beta is a different summary of the same pair of series: a slope, not the volatility of the residual gap. Two portfolios can share a beta and have very different tracking errors.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Ex post is not ex ante. The standard deviation of realised active returns is not the tracking error a covariance model would predict for the current holdings.
  • Annualisation. Multiplying a daily active-return standard deviation by sqrt(252) assumes uncorrelated active returns. A persistent active bet (a permanent sector tilt) has a tracking error that does not scale that way if you change the sampling interval without care. Be consistent about P.
  • Levels versus returns. Tracking error is defined on returns. A price spread between an ETF and its basket is a different measurement.

faq.question: Can tracking error be zero while the portfolio differs from the benchmark?
faq.answer: Yes, if the difference in returns is constant. Standard deviation does not see the mean. A constant lag of one basis point per day is a large cumulative gap and a zero tracking error.

faq.question: Is tracking error the same as active risk?
faq.answer: In mandate language, active risk usually means this volatility of active returns, sometimes the ex-ante forecast of it. Quote whether the number is realised or predicted. This function is realised.

test:
import numpy as np
port = np.array([0.02, 0.00, 0.01])
bench = np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.00])
a = port - bench
assert abs(tracking_error(port, bench) - a.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)) < 1e-12
assert tracking_error([0.25, 0.5, 0.75], [0.0, 0.25, 0.5]) == 0.0

name: Maximum Drawdown
summary: The most negative peak-to-trough decline of an equity curve. A 25 percent decline is returned as −0.25, not as 0.25.
definition: Drawdown at each point is the equity divided by the highest equity seen so far, minus one. The maximum drawdown is the smallest of those numbers (the deepest loss from a peak). It is path dependent: the order of returns matters, not only their mean and variance. The function expects a positive equity curve, not a return series.
formula:
DD_t = E_t / max_{s ≤ t} E_s − 1
MDD  = min_t DD_t

MDD ≤ 0. MDD = 0 means the equity curve never fell below a peak it had already set.
Recovery and the length of the drawdown are not part of this number.

sections.heading: Using it next to a return ratio
sections.html:
• Sharpe and Sortino compress the path into moments. Maximum drawdown keeps one fact about the path: the worst decline from a high-water mark. Report both.
  • The performance calculator uses this definition and also reports how long the longest drawdown lasted. Duration is not in the function on this page.
  • Calmar divides annualised growth by the absolute value of this number.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Sign. The function returns a non-positive fraction. Taking abs is the caller's job when a report wants "25 percent drawdown" as a positive phrase. Calmar does that internally.
  • Equity, not returns. Passing returns produces a meaningless ratio of small numbers. Compound the returns to equity first. The first point is a peak by definition, so a curve that falls immediately draws down from the starting level.
  • Sample length. A longer window can only make the maximum worse or leave it unchanged, if it contains the shorter window. Comparing a one-year MDD with a ten-year MDD as if they were the same statistic favours the short window.
  • Mark-to-market frequency. Daily equity and monthly equity do not share a maximum drawdown. Intra-month peaks are invisible on a monthly curve.

faq.question: Does the maximum drawdown say when it happened?
faq.answer: No. It is a single fraction. The performance calculator on this site also reports the peak and trough dates and the longest time spent below a peak. Those need the whole drawdown path, not only its minimum.

faq.question: What if the curve ends at its low?
faq.answer: The unrecovered decline is included. Maximum drawdown does not require the equity to have made a new high afterwards. A strategy that fell 40 percent and never recovered has a maximum drawdown of at least 40 percent.

test:
import numpy as np
assert abs(max_drawdown([100, 120, 90, 130]) - (90 / 120 - 1)) < 1e-15
assert max_drawdown([100, 101, 102]) == 0.0
try:
    max_drawdown([100, 0, 110])
    raise SystemExit("non-positive equity should fail")
except ValueError:
    pass

name: Calmar Ratio
summary: Compound annual growth of an equity curve divided by the absolute value of its maximum drawdown. This implementation uses the whole sample, not a trailing 36-month window.
definition: Calmar divides a growth rate by the worst peak-to-trough loss over the window you care about. Here the growth rate is the compound annual growth that takes the first equity point to the last, using P periods per year, and the loss is the maximum drawdown of the same points. A curve that never falls has an undefined Calmar, returned as NaN, rather than an infinite one. The original published ratio used a trailing three-year window. Using the whole sample is what the performance calculator on this site does, and it will not match a 36-month Calmar when the sample is a different length.
formula:
n = number of returns = (number of equity points) − 1
CAGR = (E_last / E_first) ^ (P / n) − 1
MDD  = min_t (E_t / max_{s≤t} E_s − 1)          MDD ≤ 0

Calmar = CAGR / |MDD|     if MDD < 0, else undefined

P defaults to 252. The same equity series should be used for the numerator and the denominator.

sections.heading: Reading it
sections.html:
• A Calmar of 0.5 means the compound annual growth was half the size of the worst decline, on this sample and this annualisation. It is not a forecast of either input.
  • The pieces are on their own pages: growth uses the same exponent as the performance calculator, and the denominator is maximum drawdown.
  • Sharpe uses a typical deviation. Calmar uses a single worst episode. One deep drawdown dominates it, which is the point of the ratio and also its instability.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Window. Young (1991) described a three-year lookback. A ten-year Calmar and a three-year Calmar of the same fund are different statistics. This function uses every point you pass.
  • Start and end dates are part of the answer. CAGR depends on the first and last equity. MDD depends on the path between them. Dropping a crash from the sample changes the denominator; ending on a peak changes the numerator.
  • Frequency. P has to match the spacing of the equity points. Passing daily equity with P = 12 treats a year of days as twelve periods.

faq.question: Why not use a 36-month window?
faq.answer: The original Calmar ratio did. This site's performance calculator divides full-sample CAGR by full-sample maximum drawdown, and the glossary function matches that so the two do not disagree. For a 36-month figure, pass only those points.

faq.question: What does NaN mean here?
faq.answer: The equity curve made no new low relative to a peak, so the denominator would be zero. That includes a curve that only rises. It is not an infinite reward-to-risk ratio.

test:
import numpy as np
eq = np.array([4.0, 2.0, 8.0])
# periods=2: CAGR = 8/4 - 1 = 1, |MDD| = 0.5, Calmar = 2
assert abs(calmar_ratio(eq, periods=2) - 2.0) < 1e-12
assert np.isnan(calmar_ratio([100.0, 110.0, 120.0]))

name: Kelly Criterion
summary: The bet size that maximises expected logarithmic growth. For a binary bet it is an exact fraction of wealth. For a continuous return it is approximately mean over variance. It is a sizing formula, not advice to use it.
definition: A log-utility investor who can repeat the same bet wants the fraction of wealth that maximises the expected log of wealth after the bet. For a binary outcome that pays net odds b with probability p, that fraction is p − (1 − p) / b. For a continuous excess return with mean μ and variance σ², the corresponding unconstrained fraction is approximately μ / σ² when the higher moments are ignored. Estimated μ and σ² are noisy, and the full fraction is aggressive when the estimate is wrong, so practitioners who use the idea often scale it down. Nothing on this page says that an investor should.
formula:
Binary bet, win probability p, net odds b (win b for each 1 staked):
  f* = p − (1 − p) / b = (b p − (1 − p)) / b

Continuous approximation, excess mean μ and variance σ² over the same horizon:
  f* ≈ μ / σ²

f* < 0 means the edge is negative: the formula says stake nothing on that side.
f* > 1 means the approximation wants leverage. The binary formula assumes you cannot stake more than wealth if you cap it; this function does not cap.

sections.heading: What the two formulas assume
sections.html:
• The binary formula is exact for one repeated i.i.d. bet with known p and b, and for an objective that only cares about expected log wealth. Change the objective and the fraction changes.
  • The continuous formula is a small-bet or diffusion approximation. It ignores skew and the chance of a loss large enough to make the log argument non-positive. A return distribution with a fat left tail is exactly where that matters.
  • Volatility in the denominator is the same object as in the Sharpe ratio, but the Kelly fraction is not a Sharpe ratio. Sharpe divides by standard deviation and annualises. Kelly divides by variance and is a weight.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The inputs are estimates. Full Kelly computed from a sample mean is famous for suggesting large weights that were an artefact of the sample. A fraction of the estimate (half Kelly, quarter Kelly) is a common ad-hoc shrink. This code does not apply one.
  • No drawdown constraint. Log growth can coexist with deep drawdowns. The formula does not know your limit.
  • Odds b are net odds. Even money is b = 1, not 2. Passing the decimal payout instead of the net profit doubles-counts the stake and shrinks f*.
  • Not a recommendation. The function returns a number from an objective. It does not say the bet is worth making.

code_snippet:
def kelly_fraction(p, b) -> float:
    """Fraction of wealth for a binary bet. p = win probability, b = net odds.

    f* = p - (1 - p) / b. Does not cap at 0 or 1. Not a recommendation to bet.
    """
    p, b = float(p), float(b)
    if not 0.0 <= p <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("p must be in [0, 1]")
    if b <= 0:
        raise ValueError("b, the net odds, must be positive")
    return p - (1.0 - p) / b

def kelly_continuous(mu, variance) -> float:
    """Approximate Kelly fraction mu / variance for a continuous excess return.

    Ignores higher moments. Not a position-sizing recommendation.
    """
    mu, variance = float(mu), float(variance)
    if variance <= 0:
        raise ValueError("variance must be positive")
    return mu / variance

faq.question: Why do people use half Kelly?
faq.answer: Because p, b, μ and σ² plugged into the formula are estimates, and the expected log growth falls off slowly just below the optimum and steeply above it. Betting less than the estimated full fraction gives up a little growth on the estimated edge and hurts less when the edge was overstated. Half is a convention, not a theorem, and this page does not apply it.

faq.question: What does a negative fraction mean?
faq.answer: For the binary bet, the probability and the odds do not compensate each other: expected log wealth is higher at a stake of zero than at a long stake. It is not an instruction to take the other side unless that side is a bet you can actually price with its own p and b.

test:
assert abs(kelly_fraction(0.6, 1.0) - 0.2) < 1e-15
assert kelly_fraction(0.4, 1.0) < 0
assert abs(kelly_continuous(0.01, 0.04) - 0.25) < 1e-15
try:
    kelly_fraction(0.6, 0)
    raise SystemExit("zero odds should fail")
except ValueError:
    pass

name: Beta
summary: The OLS slope of an asset's returns on a market's returns: covariance divided by the market's variance. It is the CAPM coefficient on the sample you pass in, not a forecast.
definition: Beta measures how much an asset's return tended to move with the market return in a sample. It is Cov(R_i, R_m) / Var(R_m), which is also the slope of a regression of the asset on the market with an intercept. A beta of 1 means the asset moved one-for-one with the market on average, after the intercept absorbed the mean difference. It says nothing, by itself, about residual risk or about whether the sample will repeat.
formula:
β = Cov(R_i, R_m) / Var(R_m)

Sample covariance and variance, ddof = 1 (the OLS slope).
The intercept α = mean(R_i) − β · mean(R_m) is not returned.
Var(R_m) = 0 → undefined; the function raises.

CAPM uses a beta against the market excess return. This function uses the two series you pass. If they are excess returns, β is the CAPM slope; if they are raw returns, it is a raw-return slope.

sections.heading: What it is not
sections.html:
• It is not correlation. Correlation divides by both standard deviations and lies in [−1, 1]. Beta is in the units of "asset return per unit of market return" and can sit far outside that interval.
  • It is not tracking error. Tracking error is the volatility of the gap. Beta is the slope. An index fund should have a beta near 1 and a small tracking error; a leveraged index fund can have a beta near 2 and still a small residual.
  • It is not the Sharpe ratio. Sharpe has no benchmark series other than cash.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Unstable in short samples. A 60-day beta and a five-year beta of the same name often disagree. The function does not shrink toward 1. If you want a shrunk beta, do it after the call and say so.
  • The market series is the definition of the beta. A national equity index, a futures excess return and a global market portfolio produce three different numbers. The symbol β does not record which one you used.
  • Changing composition. Beta of a portfolio computed from the portfolio's past returns describes the portfolio as it was, including positions it no longer holds.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np

def beta(asset, market) -> float:
    """OLS slope Cov(asset, market) / Var(market), sample moments (ddof=1)."""
    a = np.asarray(asset, dtype=float)
    m = np.asarray(market, dtype=float)
    if a.shape != m.shape or a.ndim != 1 or a.size < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two aligned returns")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(a)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(m)):
        raise ValueError("returns must be finite")
    var_m = float(np.var(m, ddof=1))
    if var_m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("market variance is zero")
    cov = float(np.cov(a, m, ddof=1)[0, 1])
    return cov / var_m

faq.question: Does beta include an intercept?
faq.answer: The slope from Cov/Var is exactly the OLS slope when an intercept is allowed. The intercept is the average return not explained by the market in that sample. This function returns only the slope.

faq.question: Why did I get a beta far from my broker's beta?
faq.answer: The window, the frequency, the market series and whether returns are excess or raw all change the slope. Two betas are comparable when those choices match. This function documents none of them except the arithmetic, which is sample covariance over sample variance.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = rng.normal(0, 0.01, 500)
a = 0.002 + 1.5 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.001, 500)
assert abs(beta(a, m) - 1.5) < 0.05
exact = np.array([0.01, -0.02, 0.015, 0.005])
assert abs(beta(1.5 * exact + 0.001, exact) - 1.5) < 1e-10
try:
    beta([0.01, 0.02], [0.01, 0.01])
    raise SystemExit("flat market should fail")
except ValueError:
    pass

name: Realized Volatility
summary: The square root of the sum of squared log returns inside one window, optionally scaled to a year. For a single day of intraday prices, multiplying by 252 annualises that day's realized variance. Do not do that to a stack of many days.
definition: Realized variance over a window is the sum of squared logarithmic returns of the prices inside it. Realized volatility is its square root. Under a diffusion with no jumps, that sum estimates the integrated variance of the window, and finer sampling makes the estimate tighter until microstructure noise dominates. The function annualises by multiplying the sum by a periods-per-year factor before the square root. That factor is correct when the sum is one period's variance (one day, if the factor is 252). Applied to a year of already-daily returns it multiplies a yearly total by 252 and overstates volatility by about sqrt(252).
formula:
r_i = ln(P_i / P_{i−1})
RV  = sqrt( (Σ_i r_i²) · P )

P = periods per year used to annualise THIS window.
One day of intraday returns → P = 252 (or 242) gives an annualised number from that day.
A window you do not want to annualise → P = 1, which returns sqrt(Σ r_i²).

The sum of squares, not the square of the sum. Signs of returns do not matter.

sections.heading: What the window is
sections.html:
• Pass the prices of one period. A session of one-minute prices in, an annualised volatility for that session out, if you set the factor to the number of sessions in a year.
  • To describe a year, compute each day's sum of squares and then average the daily realized variances, and only then scale. This function does not do that average. It scales whatever sum you hand it.
  • Close-to-close volatility is the ordinary standard deviation of daily log returns, a different estimator. Range estimators such as Parkinson use high and low. A conditional model is GARCH.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Annualisation is the easy mistake. Σ r² over 252 daily returns is already a year of variance. Multiplying by another 252 is wrong. Use P = 1 for a pre-aggregated sum you do not want scaled.
  • Microstructure. Bid-ask bounce biases the sum of squares up as the sampling gets finer. One-second returns on a wide spread mostly measure the spread.
  • Jumps and overnight. A close-to-open jump is one large r_i if you include it, and is invisible if you only pass the cash session. Neither choice is free.
  • Zeros and negative prices. Log returns require positive prices. The function rejects the rest.

faq.question: How do I annualise a year of daily realized variances?
faq.answer: Average the daily sums of squared intraday returns first (that average estimates average daily variance), then multiply by the number of sessions in a year and take the square root. Passing every intraday price of the year into this function with periods_per_year=252 multiplies a year of variance by 252.

faq.question: Why log returns?
faq.answer: Squared log returns add up to integrated variance for a diffusion. Squared simple returns are close when the moves are small and are a different estimator when they are not. The function uses logs.

name: Parkinson Volatility
summary: A volatility estimator that uses each period's high and low instead of the close-to-close move. Under a driftless Brownian motion it is more efficient than the close-to-close estimator. With drift, jumps or a close that is not the whole story, that efficiency result does not apply.
definition: Parkinson (1980) replaces the squared close-to-close return with the squared log range. The scaling 1 / (4 ln 2) makes the average of those squared ranges an estimate of the variance per period, for a Brownian motion with no drift. Multiplying by the number of periods in a year and taking the square root annualises it. The estimator never sees the open or the close. A day that gaps and then trades in a narrow range looks quiet.
formula:
σ²_period = (1 / (4 N ln 2)) · Σ_{t=1..N} (ln(H_t / L_t))²
σ_annual  = σ_period · sqrt(P)

H_t ≥ L_t > 0.  N is the number of ranges you pass.
4 ln 2 ≈ 2.7726, so a day whose high is about 1.7% above its low
(ln(H/L) ≈ 0.0166, squared ≈ 2.77e-4) contributes about 1e-4 of daily variance
before annualisation, i.e. 1 percent daily, before the average.

P defaults to 252 and scales the mean daily variance, which is the right
shape when each row is one session.

sections.heading: Why a range
sections.html:
• The high and the low summarise the whole path, not only the two endpoints. For a driftless Brownian motion the range estimator has a lower variance than the close-to-close estimator on the same number of days.
  • It is a natural check on realized volatility when you have bars but not a full trade tape: daily high and low are enough.
  • It is still a historical number. An option-implied number is implied volatility, and a recursive filter is GARCH.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Drift. A strong trend widens the range for a reason other than diffusion variance. Parkinson is derived at zero drift. Rogers-Satchell and Yang-Zhang exist because of that; this page does not implement them.
  • Overnight gaps. If high and low are the cash-session extrema, the gap from yesterday's close is invisible. The estimator then misses a piece of the day's variance that a close-to-close number includes.
  • Bad prints. One erroneous high dominates a squared range. The average does not trim it.
  • Do not feed intraday bars and also multiply by 252 unless each row is one session. The function annualises the mean of the rows you pass.

faq.question: Why is the divisor 4 ln 2?
faq.answer: It is the expected value of the squared log range of a standard Brownian motion over one unit of time. Dividing by it converts an average squared range into a variance estimate. The derivation assumes no drift and no jumps.

faq.question: Is Parkinson always better than close-to-close?
faq.answer: No. It is more efficient in the zero-drift diffusion it was derived for. A large overnight gap, a trading halt, or a bad high print can make it worse than a close-to-close estimator that at least uses the official closes.

low = np.ones(10)

name: GARCH(1,1)
summary: A conditional variance that is a constant plus a weight on yesterday's squared shock plus a weight on yesterday's variance. This page filters a series with given parameters. It does not estimate them.
definition: GARCH(1,1), Bollerslev (1986), says today's variance depends on a long-run piece, on how large yesterday's surprise was, and on yesterday's variance. Clusters of large moves follow because a large shock raises the next variance, which keeps later variances high until the β term decays. The function below runs that recursion. ω, α and β are inputs. Fitting them by maximum likelihood is a numerical problem this page does not solve. The variance at step 0 is the first squared return, so the filter does not use later data to start itself.
formula:
σ²_t = ω + α ε²_{t−1} + β σ²_{t−1}

σ²_0 = ε_0²          (a one-point start; not the sample variance of the whole series)
Unconditional variance, when α ≥ 0, β ≥ 0 and α + β < 1:
  σ²_∞ = ω / (1 − α − β)

α + β is the persistence. α + β ≥ 1 means there is no finite unconditional variance.
The filter still runs. Half-life of a shock to variance is about ln(2) / −ln(α+β) periods when α+β < 1.

EWMA is the case ω = 0, α + β = 1, with α = 1−λ and β = λ. See the Numba EWMA page.

sections.heading: Filter versus estimate
sections.html:
• Given parameters, the recursion is a one-pass filter. That is what garch11_variance does, and what the tests check.
  • The parameters themselves are usually estimated by maximising a Gaussian or Student-t likelihood. Different likelihoods, different estimates. Publishing a 20-line fitter here would hide that choice.
  • Compare the path with realized volatility (a sum of squares, no parameters) and with EWMA (persistence fixed at 1).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The shock is the return only if the mean is zero. The recursion treats the series you pass as ε. If you meant a demeaned residual, demean first. A large mean inside ε² looks like volatility.
  • Starting value. ε_0² can be a wild first day. An alternative is the unconditional variance, which depends on the parameters and, if those were fit on this same sample, uses the whole sample. This filter does not do that.
  • α + β close to 1 makes the unconditional variance huge and the filter slow to forget. Integrated GARCH (α + β = 1) never forgets a shock in the level of variance.
  • No leverage term. Plain GARCH treats an up move and a down move of the same size identically. GJR and EGARCH exist because equity returns usually do not.

faq.question: Why not fit the parameters on this page?
faq.answer: A Gaussian likelihood, a Student-t likelihood and a robust estimator do not return the same (ω, α, β), and the optimiser needs constraints so that variances stay positive. The recursion itself is the part that can be checked exactly. Bring parameters from a fit you trust.

faq.question: Is the variance at t allowed to use the return at t?
faq.answer: Not in this filter. σ²_t is the variance assigned before ε_t is treated as realised, which is what you want if the next step is to standardise ε_t by σ_t. The update that includes ε_t² lands in σ²_{t+1}.

name: Implied Volatility
summary: The volatility that makes a Black-Scholes-Merton price match an observed option premium. It is solved numerically. There is no closed form for the call price inverted in volatility.
definition: Implied volatility is defined by an equation, not by a formula you can rearrange. Given a market premium, a spot, a strike, a time to expiry, a rate and a dividend yield, it is the σ that sets the Black-Scholes-Merton price equal to that premium. This page solves it with Brent's method on a bracket. The same inversion, across strikes and expiries, is what the smile tool on this site plots. A single number always belongs to one contract and one set of inputs.
formula:
C_BSM(S, K, T, r, q, σ_imp) = C_market

d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)
d2 = d1 − σ √T
C  = S e^{−qT} N(d1) − K e^{−rT} N(d2)

No-arbitrage range for a European call, before the solve:
  max(S e^{−qT} − K e^{−rT}, 0) ≤ C ≤ S e^{−qT}
A premium outside that range has no real implied volatility.

sections.heading: Solving it
sections.html:
• The call price increases in σ, so the root is unique when it exists. Brent's method needs a bracket. The code starts at 0.000001 and 5 (500 percent) and widens to 20 if the premium is still above the model at 5.
  • A premium that sits on intrinsic value returns 0. A premium outside the no-arbitrage bounds raises, rather than returning a quiet NaN that looks like a failed fit.
  • The implied-volatility smile tool solves the same inversion across a grid and fits a slope. One contract's σ_imp is the building block. Vega is how the price moves when that input moves.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The model is part of the answer. A Black-Scholes implied volatility and a Black-76 implied volatility on the same premium are not the same number. This page is Black-Scholes-Merton with a continuous dividend yield q. Set q = 0 for the textbook no-dividend call.
  • European, one expiry, constant inputs. American early exercise, discrete dividends and a volatility that depends on the strike are all outside the inverter. The smile is exactly the evidence that one σ does not price every strike.
  • Deep, short-dated options. Vega collapses and many volatilities map to almost the same premium. The root is mathematically there and practically poorly identified. Trust the price residual, not just the σ.

faq.question: Why is there no formula for implied volatility?
faq.answer: The cumulative normal of d1 and d2 depends on σ in a way that does not invert in closed form. Series approximations exist. A bracketed root find on a monotone function is the straightforward exact method, and it is what this page tests.

faq.question: Does a higher implied volatility mean the option is expensive?
faq.answer: It means the premium is high relative to this model's other inputs. Whether that is expensive depends on the volatility you believe the underlying will actually realise, on the smile, and on costs. The number itself is a restatement of the premium.

name: Delta
summary: The derivative of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value with respect to the spot. A call delta is e^{−qT} N(d1). A put delta is that quantity minus e^{−qT}.
definition: Delta is how much the model value changes for a small move in the underlying, holding the other inputs fixed. In Black-Scholes-Merton it is a closed form. For a call it lies between 0 and e^{−qT}; for a put it lies between −e^{−qT} and 0. With no dividend yield those bounds are 0 and 1, and −1 and 0. The figure is a model sensitivity. Hedging with it leaves everything the model left out, including jumps and the fact that volatility is not a constant.
formula:
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Δ_call = e^{−qT} N(d1)
Δ_put  = e^{−qT} (N(d1) − 1) = −e^{−qT} N(−d1)

Δ_call − Δ_put = e^{−qT}

q = 0 is the no-dividend textbook case: Δ_call = N(d1), Δ_put = N(d1) − 1.
The on-site calculator uses the same expressions, including q.

sections.heading: How to read the number
sections.html:
• A call delta of 0.50 is not automatically at-the-money once rates or dividends are nonzero. It is the model slope at those inputs. N(d1) equals a half when d1 is zero, which is not the same as S = K.
  • Delta of a position is the sum of signed deltas times the multiplier. The function returns the per-unit derivative, not a share count for a book.
  • The slope changes as spot moves. That second derivative is gamma. The slope also depends on the volatility you typed in, which is where implied volatility enters.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• European Black-Scholes-Merton only. American puts, barriers and anything path dependent do not have this delta. At expiry the slope becomes a step. The Greeks calculator spells out that limit; this function requires T > 0 and σ > 0 so the formula stays the smooth one.
  • Spot delta versus forward delta. The derivative here is with respect to spot, and it includes the dividend discount e^{−qT}. A forward delta omits that discount. Mixing them mis-hedges by that factor.
  • A hedge ratio is not a hedge result. Replacing the option with −Δ shares cancels the first-order spot term in this model, at this instant. Gamma, vega and discrete rebalancing remain.

code_snippet:
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_delta(S, K, T, r, sigma, call=True, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton spot delta. call=False returns the put delta.

    Requires positive S, K, T and sigma. q is a continuous dividend yield.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    disc = exp(-q * T)
    return float(disc * norm.cdf(d1) if call else disc * (norm.cdf(d1) - 1.0))

faq.question: Why is call delta not exactly N(d1)?
faq.answer: N(d1) is the no-dividend formula. With a continuous yield q the spot delta of a European call is e^{−qT} N(d1). The two agree when q is 0, which is the default of this function.

faq.question: Does delta tell me the probability the option finishes in the money?
faq.answer: No. Under the stock-numeraire measure, N(d1) is a probability related to the share, and N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability that a European call finishes in the money, in this model, with no dividends changing that statement. Neither one is a real-world probability, and neither one is a trading instruction.

d_call = bs_delta(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, True, 0.0)
d_put = bs_delta(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, False, 0.0)
assert abs(d_call - 0.6368306511756191) < 1e-9
assert abs(d_put - (-0.3631693488243809)) < 1e-9
assert abs(d_call - d_put - 1.0) < 1e-12

name: Gamma
summary: The second derivative of a European option's value with respect to the spot, and the derivative of delta. In Black-Scholes-Merton the call and the put of the same strike and expiry have the same gamma.
definition: Gamma tells you how fast delta changes as the spot moves. It is largest near the strike and near expiry, where the distribution of finishing in or out of the money is most sensitive to the current spot. Because a European call and put that share strike and expiry differ by a forward (put-call parity), and a forward has no gamma, their gammas are equal. The formula below is that common value.
formula:
Γ = e^{−qT} φ(d1) / (S σ √T)

φ is the standard normal density.
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Same number for the European call and the European put.
Units: change in delta per 1 point of spot. Not a percent.

sections.heading: Why the call and the put match
sections.html:
• Put-call parity says the call minus the put equals a discounted forward. Differentiating twice in S kills the forward and leaves Γ_call = Γ_put.
  • Delta does not match. The call delta and the put delta differ by e^{−qT}. See delta.
  • The Greeks calculator reports this gamma for both sides.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• It blows up as expiry approaches for an option sitting on the strike, because of the √T in the denominator, and it goes to 0 for an option far from the strike. A gamma number with no spot, strike and expiry attached is not interpretable.
  • P&L is not gamma times the move. The second-order Taylor term is ½ Γ (ΔS)², and it is a model term. Realised moves, hedges and vega P&L are all still there.
  • Spot gamma. As with delta, this differentiates with respect to spot and includes e^{−qT}. Divide by that discount if you wanted a forward gamma and you meant to.

faq.question: Why does gamma not depend on whether the option is a call or a put?
faq.answer: Call minus put is a forward under put-call parity, and a forward's second derivative with respect to spot is zero. Whatever curvature the call has, the put has the same curvature.

faq.question: Is a high gamma good?
faq.answer: It means delta will move quickly if the spot moves, which is a property of that contract in this model. Long gamma and short gamma describe a position. The page does not score either as an advantage.

test:

from scipy.stats import norm
g = bs_gamma(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.0)
assert abs(g - 0.018762017345846895) < 1e-9

def call_delta(S):
    T, r, sigma, q, K = 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.0, 100.0
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    return exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(d1)

eps = 1e-2
fd = (call_delta(100 + eps) - call_delta(100 - eps)) / (2 * eps)
assert abs(g - fd) / g < 1e-6

name: Vega
summary: The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to volatility, quoted per volatility point (one percentage point of σ). Call and put vegas of the same contract are equal.
definition: Vega is the derivative of the model price with respect to the volatility input. A raw derivative is per 1.00 of σ, that is, per 100 volatility points, which is an awkward unit. Dividing by 100 quotes the change in premium for a one-point move in volatility, the convention used by the Greeks calculator on this site. Because of put-call parity, a European call and put with the same strike and expiry have the same vega: the forward that separates them does not depend on σ.
formula:
ν_raw = S e^{−qT} φ(d1) √T          per 1.00 of volatility
ν     = ν_raw / 100                  per 1 volatility point

d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)
Same value for the European call and the European put.
φ is the standard normal density.

sections.heading: Units
sections.html:
• If the model price rises by 0.375 when volatility goes from 20 percent to 21 percent, vega per point is about 0.375. The raw derivative ∂V/∂σ is about 37.5. This function returns the per-point number.
  • The Greeks calculator divides by 100 in the same place. Implied volatility is the σ that the premium implies; vega is how the premium would change if that input changed.
  • Call and put share vega for the same reason they share gamma: their difference is a forward.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Volatility point means 0.01 in decimal σ. Moving σ from 0.20 to 0.21 is one point. Moving it from 0.20 to 1.20 is one hundred points.
  • Sticky strike, sticky delta, and the smile. The derivative holds every other input fixed, including a single σ. On a smile, a spot move often comes with a different implied volatility. Model vega does not include that.
  • Near expiry, deep in or out of the money, vega is small. Many vols then fit almost the same premium, which is the same fact as a flat price-versus-σ curve.

faq.question: Why divide by 100?
faq.answer: The calculus derivative is the change in price for a change of 1.00 in σ, i.e. from 20 percent to 120 percent. Desks quote the change for one point, from 20 percent to 21 percent, which is that derivative divided by 100. The calculator on this site does the same.

faq.question: Do calls and puts have the same vega?
faq.answer: European calls and puts with the same strike and expiry do, in Black-Scholes-Merton. Put-call parity says their difference does not depend on volatility, so the volatility derivatives match.

from scipy.stats import norm

name: Theta
summary: The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to the passage of calendar time, quoted per day. The annual derivative is divided by 365.
definition: Theta is the derivative of the model value with respect to calendar time, holding spot, volatility, rates and yield fixed. Time to expiry shrinks as calendar time advances, so the formula is minus the derivative with respect to T, then divided by 365 to quote a per-day number. Long options usually have negative theta: the premium decays as expiry approaches, all else equal. That "all else equal" is the catch. Spot and implied volatility do not stay still so that theta can be observed on its own.
formula:
Let φ(d1) be the standard normal density, and
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T),   d2 = d1 − σ √T.

Θ_call = [ −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) − r K e^{−rT} N(d2) + q S e^{−qT} N(d1) ] / 365
Θ_put  = [ −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) + r K e^{−rT} N(−d2) − q S e^{−qT} N(−d1) ] / 365

Both are per calendar day. A trading-day theta divides the annual derivative by 252 instead;
multiply the value here by 365/252 to convert. q = 0 drops the last term in each bracket.
The Greeks calculator on this site uses these expressions.

sections.heading: What the sign means
sections.html:
• Negative theta means the model value falls as the clock runs, with every other input frozen. That is the usual case for a long option away from unusual rate and dividend combinations.
  • The decay term −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) is shared. The rate and dividend terms differ for calls and puts, which is why a call theta and a put theta are not equal, unlike gamma and vega.
  • See delta for the d1 that enters, and the Greeks calculator for the same per-day convention.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• 365 versus 252. This function divides by 365, calendar days, matching the calculator. A desk that marks theta per trading day wants the other divisor. The two numbers differ by 365/252.
  • One day is not infinitesimal. The derivative times 1/365 approximates the change from losing one calendar day of expiry. Very short-dated options have a theta that changes a lot over that same day, so the approximation is rougher.
  • Frozen volatility. The derivative does not include a change in implied volatility as expiry approaches. Real premiums move for that reason too.

code_snippet:
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_theta(S, K, T, r, sigma, call=True, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton theta per calendar day (annual derivative / 365).

    call=False returns the put. Multiply by 365/252 for a trading-day theta.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    sT = sigma * sqrt(T)
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / sT
    d2 = d1 - sT
    decay = -S * exp(-q * T) * norm.pdf(d1) * sigma / (2.0 * sqrt(T))
    if call:
        annual = decay - r * K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2) + q * S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(d1)
    else:
        annual = decay + r * K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(-d2) - q * S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(-d1)
    return float(annual / 365.0)

faq.question: Why is theta usually negative for a long option?
faq.answer: With the other inputs held fixed, less time means less chance of a large move and, for a call, less time for the prepaid forward to earn its rates. The model premium of a long option therefore usually falls as expiry gets closer. A short option has the opposite sign. This is a partial derivative, not a prediction of tomorrow's premium.

faq.question: Does the function use trading days or calendar days?
faq.answer: Calendar days. The annual Black-Scholes derivative is divided by 365, which is what the Greeks calculator on this site displays. Multiply by 365/252 if you want a per-trading-day figure.

from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm
th = bs_theta(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, True, 0.0)
assert abs(th - (-0.01757267820941972)) < 1e-9

def call(T):
    S, K, r, sigma, q = 100.0, 100.0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.0
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * sqrt(T)
    return S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(d1) - K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)

assert abs((call(1 - 1 / 365) - call(1.0)) - th) < 1e-4
assert bs_theta(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, False, 0.0) != th

name: Rho
summary: The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to the continuous risk-free rate, quoted per one percentage point of rate.
definition: Rho is the derivative of the model price with respect to the interest rate, holding spot, strike, time, volatility and dividend yield fixed. Dividing by 100 quotes it per one percentage point (from 5 percent to 6 percent, for example), matching the Greeks calculator on this site. A European call's rho is positive: a higher rate lowers the present value of the strike you might pay. A European put's rho is negative. Dividend yield q is a different input and is not what this derivative moves.
formula:
ρ_call = K T e^{−rT} N(d2) / 100
ρ_put  = −K T e^{−rT} N(−d2) / 100

d2 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q − σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Per 1 percentage point of r. The raw derivative ∂V/∂r is 100 times larger.
q enters d2. It does not appear as its own discount in the rho formula;
∂V/∂q is a different Greek.

sections.heading: Sign
sections.html:
• Call rho is greater than or equal to zero in this model. Put rho is less than or equal to zero. A book that is long calls and short puts of the same strike picks up both.
  • The rate inside Black-Scholes is the continuous risk-free rate used to discount the strike, not a credit spread and not the dividend. Changing q instead is not rho.
  • The Greeks calculator reports rho per 1 percent with the formulas above. Put-call parity is where that discount shows up as K e^{−rT}.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• One point of rate, not one point of volatility. The /100 here is the same kind of unit choice as vega, applied to r rather than to σ.
  • Short-dated options have small rho because of the factor T. A one-week option barely changes when the rate moves by a point. A five-year option moves much more, in the model.
  • The rate is flat and constant. A real curve has many rates. One rho cannot describe a shift of a single tenor, a slope change, and a parallel move as three different risks.

faq.question: Why is put rho negative?
faq.answer: A higher risk-free rate reduces the present value of the strike the put might receive, and it raises the forward. Both hurt the model value of a European put, so the derivative is negative. A European call is helped by the same two facts.

faq.question: Does rho include dividend sensitivity?
faq.answer: No. q is held fixed. Rho moves only r. The dividend yield changes d2, so a different q produces a different rho, but the derivative itself is with respect to the interest rate.

from scipy.stats import norm
rc = bs_rho(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, True, 0.0)
rp = bs_rho(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2, False, 0.0)
assert abs(rc - 0.5323248154537634) < 1e-9
assert rp < 0

def call(r):
    S, K, T, sigma, q = 100.0, 100.0, 1.0, 0.2, 0.0
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * sqrt(T)
    return S * norm.cdf(d1) - K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)

assert abs((call(0.06) - call(0.04)) / 2 - rc) < 1e-3

name: Put-Call Parity
summary: A model-free relation between European call and put prices that share a strike and an expiry. With a continuous dividend yield, the call minus the put equals the prepaid forward minus the discounted strike.
definition: Put-call parity says that a long European call and a short European put, same strike and expiry, replicate a long forward position struck at K. Rearranged, the call premium minus the put premium equals the spot discounted by the dividend yield, minus the strike discounted by the interest rate. No volatility, no distribution of returns and no pricing model enters. If the two premiums violate the equation by more than transaction costs, the packages are different prices for the same payoff. The function returns the gap, which is zero when parity holds.

sections.heading: What it constrains
sections.html:
• You can back a forward out of the two premiums, which is what the smile tool does before it reads a smile off strikes. A bad forward makes every implied volatility look skewed.
  • It forces several Greeks into pairs. Differentiating in S gives Δ_call − Δ_put = e^{−qT} (delta). Differentiating in σ gives equal vegas. Differentiating twice in S gives equal gammas.
  • Rho is the sensitivity to the r that discounts K in this identity.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• European, same strike, same expiry, same underlying. An American put can be worth more than parity allows, because early exercise has value. A gap on American prices is not automatically an arbitrage.
  • Dividends have to be in q, or the identity is the wrong one. A discrete cash dividend is not a continuous yield. Using q = 0 on a stock that pays a dividend shows a gap that is just the dividend.
  • Costs. A gap smaller than the round-trip spread, fees and borrow is not a trade. The function returns a price difference, not an executable profit.

faq.question: Why does parity not mention volatility?
faq.answer: The call-minus-put package pays S_T − K at expiry no matter what path volatility takes. Its present value is the prepaid forward minus the discounted strike. Volatility changes the call and the put by the same amount, so it drops out of the difference.

faq.question: What does a non-zero gap mean?
faq.answer: At these inputs the two premiums are not consistent with one forward. Causes include a dividend yield you left at zero, American early exercise, stale quotes, or a genuine dislocation larger than the cost of putting the package on. The sign says which side is rich relative to the identity. It does not by itself say there is a trade.

name: Half-Life of Mean Reversion
summary: How many periods an AR(1) deviation takes to decay halfway, read off the slope of a regression of changes on lagged levels. The same discrete definition as the half-life on the ADF page.
definition: Fit the regression Δy_t = a + g y_{t−1} + ε_t. The autoregressive level coefficient is φ = 1 + g. When g is between −1 and 0, the series pulls back toward its mean, and the number of periods required for a deviation to fall by half is ln 2 / −ln(1 + g). That is the discrete half-life. The continuous approximation −ln 2 / g is close only when g is near zero; at φ = 0.9 it is already about 5 percent longer than the discrete number. If g is not negative, the series is not mean-reverting on this regression and the half-life is infinite.
formula:
Δy_t = a + g · y_{t−1} + ε_t
φ = 1 + g

half-life = ln(2) / −ln(1 + g)     if −1 < g < 0
          = ∞                       if g ≥ 0
          undefined (NaN)           if g ≤ −1  (oscillatory or explosive)

Continuous approximation, small g:  ln(2) / −g
Example: φ = 0.9 → g = −0.1 → half-life = ln(2) / −ln(0.9) ≈ 6.58 periods.
The ADF page uses this discrete definition, not ln(2) / −g.

sections.heading: Where the number is used
sections.html:
• As a holding-period scale for a spread that has already passed a stationarity check. See ADF and cointegration. A half-life of six days and a half-life of six months are different research problems.
  • As a way to set the window on a rolling z-score. A window much shorter than the half-life mostly fits noise; a window of many half-lives averages different regimes.
  • Hurst is a related but different summary of the same wish: H below one half suggests anti-persistence. It is not a half-life.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Use the discrete form. Dividing ln 2 by −g treats g as a continuous-time speed. The regression you just ran is discrete. This function matches the half-life already published on the ADF page, ln 2 / −ln(1+g).
  • The regression is not a proof of mean reversion. A short sample of a random walk often produces a slightly negative g. Pair the half-life with an ADF or cointegration test, and expect the estimate to move when you add data.
  • An intercept is included. The mean that the series reverts to is −a/g, not necessarily zero. Forcing the regression through the origin changes g.
  • Not a trading rule. A finite half-life is a sample statistic. It does not say the spread will keep reverting, or that a position sized to it is desirable.

faq.question: Why not use −ln(2) / g, which is the formula many notes quote?
faq.answer: That is the continuous-time limit. The regression Δy_t = a + g y_{t−1} implies a discrete autoregressive coefficient φ = 1 + g, and a deviation multiplies by φ each period. Halving means φ^h = 1/2, so h = ln(2) / −ln(φ). At φ = 0.9 the continuous shortcut is about 6.93 periods and the discrete half-life is about 6.58.

faq.question: What half-life should a pairs trade use?
faq.answer: This page does not pick one. It estimates a half-life from the series you pass. Whether the residual is stationary, whether both legs can be traded, and what it costs are separate questions; a finite estimate is not a signal to trade the spread.

test:
import numpy as np
x = 0.9 ** np.arange(40, dtype=float)
assert abs(half_life(x) - np.log(2) / -np.log(0.9)) < 1e-8
assert half_life(np.ones(20)) == float("inf")
# Continuous shortcut is the wrong number at phi = 0.9.
assert abs((-np.log(2) / -0.1) - np.log(2) / -np.log(0.9)) > 0.3

name: O(n) Rolling Mean (Cython Memoryview Recurrence)
summary: The expanding-then-fixed rolling mean from a boundscheck-free Cython memoryview loop, implemented here with a NumPy prefix sum so the generator can re-execute it. The Cython source is included for compilation on a machine with a C toolchain.
definition: A rolling mean can be updated by adding the new observation and subtracting the one that left the window, which is a single pass. Before the window is full the same sum is divided by the number of observations seen so far. The Cython form types the buffer as a double memoryview and turns bounds checks off. This page publishes that recurrence as a tested NumPy function, plus the Cython source as a string, because this site's generator executes every snippet with CPython and cannot compile cimport.
formula:
Let s_−1 = 0. For i = 0..n−1:
  s_i = s_{i−1} + x_i − x_{i−w} · 1{i ≥ w}
  m_i = s_i / w            if i ≥ w
      = s_i / (i+1)        if i < w

Prefix-sum form (same values):
  m_i = (c_i − c_{i−w}) / w    for i ≥ w,   c_i = Σ_{k=0..i} x_k,  c_{<0} = 0
  m_i = c_i / (i+1)            for i < w

Cython sketch (compile with cythonize; not executed by the generator):
  @cython.boundscheck(False)
  @cython.wraparound(False)
  def fast_rolling_mean(double[:] arr, int window): ...

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.html:
• One rolling mean over a long tick or bar array, where a Python per-window loop is the cost and a C compiler is available for the memoryview version.
  • As a readable specification of the partial-window convention (divide by i+1 until the window is full, then by w). The NumPy function is what the tests lock in.
  • For several rolling statistics at once, or for prices with a large level, the centred running sums in rolling-window-numba are a better fit. They need no compiler and lose less precision.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• This page does not compile Cython. cimport is not valid Python, so shipping only the memoryview function would fail the rebuild test. CYTHON_SOURCE is the compiled form; fast_rolling_mean is the reference.
  • Cancellation. A raw running sum of prices near 10,000 loses digits in the variance, and even the mean drifts once the sum is huge. Re-centre, or use the Numba operators, if the level is large relative to the variation inside the window.
  • NaNs. One NaN stays inside the prefix sum from that index onward. Drop or fill gaps first.
  • Window edges. Index i = w−1 is still the mean of the first w points. Index i = w drops x_0. Callers who want NaN during the warm-up should mask i < w−1 themselves.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np

# Same recurrence as a Cython loop over a double memoryview. Compile CYTHON_SOURCE
# with Cython (boundscheck and wraparound off) when a C compiler is available.
# The function below is the tested reference: CPython cannot execute cimport.
CYTHON_SOURCE = """
cimport cython
import numpy as np

@cython.boundscheck(False)
@cython.wraparound(False)
def fast_rolling_mean(double[:] arr, int window):
    cdef int n = arr.shape[0]
    cdef double[:] res = np.empty(n)
    cdef double s = 0.0
    cdef int i
    for i in range(n):
        s += arr[i]
        if i >= window:
            s -= arr[i - window]
            res[i] = s / window
        else:
            res[i] = s / (i + 1)
    return np.asarray(res)
"""

def fast_rolling_mean(arr, window: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rolling mean. Partial windows divide by the number of points seen so far.

    For i >= window the result is the mean of x[i-window+1 : i+1].
    Equivalent to the memoryview loop in CYTHON_SOURCE.
    """
    x = np.ascontiguousarray(arr, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1)
    window = int(window)
    if window < 1:
        raise ValueError("window must be a positive integer")
    n = x.size
    out = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    if n == 0:
        return out
    csum = np.cumsum(x)
    np.divide(csum, np.arange(1, n + 1, dtype=np.float64), out=out)
    if n > window:
        out[window:] = (csum[window:] - csum[:-window]) / window
    return out

faq.question: Why is the published function NumPy rather than Cython?
faq.answer: The site rebuilds by executing every snippet with Python. Cython syntax such as cimport and cdef does not run there, and a C compiler is not part of the rebuild. The NumPy prefix sum matches the memoryview loop value for value; the Cython source is in the same file for when you compile it locally.

faq.question: How is this different from the Numba rolling operators?
faq.answer: This recurrence is a single mean, including a defined value on the warm-up samples. The Numba snippet computes mean, sample standard deviation, rolling beta and a 2-D z-score, re-centres to protect precision, and leaves the warm-up as NaN.

name: Load Hive-Partitioned Parquet Ticks with Bound Parameters
summary: Read a date slice of tick Parquet through DuckDB. The file glob and the date are bound parameters, so a path or a date string cannot change the SQL.
definition: DuckDB queries Parquet in place. With Hive layout (one folder per day), a predicate on the partition column skips other days. The glob passed to read_parquet and the date in the WHERE clause are both placeholders. Building either value into the SQL text with an f-string would let a quote in a path, or a crafted date, close the string and append another statement. Binding them does not.
formula:
Layout:  ticks/date=YYYY-MM-DD/part-*.parquet
Columns: timestamp, symbol, price, volume

SELECT symbol, timestamp, price, volume
FROM read_parquet(?, hive_partitioning = true)   -- ? = glob, not an interpolated path
WHERE date = ?                                   -- ? = the date
  AND volume > 0
ORDER BY timestamp

sections.heading: Why bind every value
sections.html:
• The date filter is what makes a Hive layout useful: folders outside the day are not opened. It only stays a filter if it is a value, not a piece of SQL text.
  • Paths from a config file, a request, or a folder name with a quote are data. read_parquet(?) passes them through DuckDB's parameter API.
  • For minute bars, VWAP and code filters on the same layout, see duckdb-parquet-ticks.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Partition type. Hive values are parsed from folder names. date=2024-03-01 usually arrives as a date. Compare it to a date or an ISO date string, and check with DESCRIBE if a filter suddenly matches nothing.
  • Zero-size prints. The query drops volume <= 0. Those rows are not trades. Decide separately whether auction prints belong in the extract.
  • Glob, not a Python path join inside SQL. Pass the glob from Python (dir/**/*.parquet). Do not concatenate it into the query string.

code_snippet:
import duckdb

def query_ticks_by_date(parquet_glob: str, target_date: str):
    """Ticks for one Hive date partition.

    parquet_glob and target_date are bound parameters. They are never
    interpolated into the SQL text.
    """
    if not isinstance(parquet_glob, str) or not isinstance(target_date, str):
        raise TypeError("parquet_glob and target_date must be strings")
    if parquet_glob == "" or target_date == "":
        raise ValueError("parquet_glob and target_date must be non-empty")
    con = duckdb.connect()
    return con.execute(
        """
        SELECT symbol, timestamp, price, volume
        FROM read_parquet(?, hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date = ?
          AND volume > 0
        ORDER BY timestamp
        """,
        [parquet_glob, target_date],
    ).df()

faq.question: Why not use an f-string for the path?
faq.answer: read_parquet needs a path, and an f-string is the obvious way to supply it, but the path then becomes SQL syntax. A directory name containing a quote breaks the query or changes it. A bound parameter keeps the path as a value. The same applies to the date.

faq.question: Does this load the whole dataset into memory?
faq.answer: DuckDB reads the Parquet row groups required by the query. A selective date predicate on a Hive partition avoids opening other days. The result of this particular query is still a pandas DataFrame of every matching tick, so aggregate in SQL when the day is large. See the minute-bar query on the DuckDB ticks page.

name: Polars Moving-Average Crossover, Lagged One Bar
summary: A moving-average crossover in Polars lazy expressions. The position is shifted one bar so it cannot earn the return that formed the signal, and a cost is charged when the position changes. Educational example only.
definition: The signal is long when the fast mean of close is above the slow mean, and flat otherwise. That decision is delayed by one bar before it multiplies returns, which is the minimum delay that removes same-bar look-ahead on a close-to-close return. Turnover is the absolute change in position. Cost is turnover times a constant in basis points. This is a single-series illustration, not a portfolio backtest and not a trading recommendation.
formula:
ret_t     = C_t / C_{t−1} − 1
signal_t  = 1{ MA_fast(C)_t > MA_slow(C)_t }     (0 while either mean is null)
pos_t     = signal_{t−1}                         (0 at t = 0)
cost_t    = |pos_t − pos_{t−1}| · cost_bps / 10^4
strat_t   = pos_t · ret_t − cost_t
equity_t  = Π_{s≤t} (1 + strat_s)

Warm-up bars, where a mean is missing, contribute signal 0.

sections.heading: What the lag does
sections.html:
• The means at bar t use the close of bar t. The return of bar t is the move from t−1 to t, which is already in that close. Multiplying them on the same row would book a fill at a price the signal has already used.
  • shift(1) applies the decision from bar t to the return of bar t+1: the earliest close-to-close return that starts after the signal.
  • For a dates × stocks book with suspensions and limit-up or limit-down flags, use vectorized-backtest. This page is one series and no trading constraints.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Costs are a flat bps charge. There is no spread, no impact and no borrow. A crossover that looks fine here can be negative once those are added.
  • One position, all or nothing. The position is 0 or 1. It does not size by volatility or cap turnover.
  • Adjusted prices. Splits and dividends have to be in the close series already. A raw close series invents returns on corporate actions.
  • This is not a forecast. A historical equity curve of a moving-average rule is a description of that sample. It is not evidence that the rule will make money on the next sample.

code_snippet:
import polars as pl

def ma_crossover_backtest(df: pl.DataFrame, fast: int = 20, slow: int = 100, cost_bps: float = 1.0) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Moving-average crossover on columns timestamp, close.

    The position implied by bar t is applied to the return of bar t+1.
    cost_bps is charged on the absolute change in position.
    Educational example only; not a trading strategy.
    """
    if fast < 1 or slow < 1:
        raise ValueError("fast and slow windows must be positive")
    if cost_bps < 0:
        raise ValueError("cost_bps must be non-negative")
    ready = pl.col("fast_ma").is_not_null() & pl.col("slow_ma").is_not_null()
    signal = pl.when(ready & (pl.col("fast_ma") > pl.col("slow_ma"))).then(1.0).otherwise(0.0)
    return (
        df.lazy()
        .sort("timestamp")
        .with_columns(
            ret=pl.col("close").pct_change(),
            fast_ma=pl.col("close").rolling_mean(fast),
            slow_ma=pl.col("close").rolling_mean(slow),
        )
        .with_columns(pos=signal.shift(1).fill_null(0.0))
        .with_columns(cost=pl.col("pos").diff().abs().fill_null(0.0) * cost_bps / 1e4)
        .with_columns(strat_ret=pl.col("pos") * pl.col("ret").fill_null(0.0) - pl.col("cost"))
        .with_columns(equity=(1 + pl.col("strat_ret")).cum_prod())
        .collect()
    )

faq.question: Why is the position shifted by one bar?
faq.answer: The close that updates the moving averages is the same close that ends the bar's return. Using the signal on that same return treats the bar as both the information and the fill. The shift makes the signal wait for the next return.

faq.question: Does a higher equity curve mean the rule works?
faq.answer: No. The curve is the result of this rule, this cost and this sample, with no market impact. Use it to check the code. Judging whether a rule is worth trading needs a later sample, realistic costs and a risk report.

name: RiskMetrics EWMA Volatility in Numba
summary: Exponentially weighted variance compiled with Numba. The variance at t uses returns only through t−1, so the latest shock is not included in the volatility assigned to that same index.
definition: RiskMetrics writes today's variance as a blend of yesterday's variance and yesterday's squared return. The weight on the previous variance is λ, often 0.94 for daily data. The square root of that variance is the EWMA volatility. The loop is a prefix recursion, which Numba compiles to a tight machine-code pass. It is a smoother with a fixed λ, not a fitted GARCH model.
formula:
σ²_0 = r_0²
σ²_t = λ σ²_{t−1} + (1 − λ) r_{t−1}²     t = 1..n−1
σ_t  = sqrt(σ²_t)

σ_t depends on r_0 .. r_{t−1} only.
0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.  λ = 1 repeats σ²_0.  λ = 0 gives σ²_t = r_{t−1}².

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.html:
• A causal volatility estimate on a long return series, for scaling positions or for comparing with realized volatility.
  • Inside another @njit loop. A Python EWMA over millions of bars spends its time in the interpreter; this one does not, after the first compile.
  • For a variance that also reacts to a long-run level and is estimated rather than set, see GARCH(1,1).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Initial value. σ²_0 = r_0² is one observation. A large first return leaves a long tail when λ is close to 1. Some desks seed the recursion with a sample variance of an earlier window instead.
  • Look-ahead. Using r_t² inside σ_t would mix the return you are about to score with the volatility you score it by. This recursion does not do that. Do not "fix" the index.
  • λ is not estimated here. 0.94 is the RiskMetrics daily convention, not a maximum-likelihood estimate for your sample. The half-life of a shock is about ln(0.5)/ln(λ) periods (about 11 days at 0.94).
  • NaNs and the first call. A NaN poisons every later value. The first call compiles; cache=True reuses the compiled code afterwards.

faq.question: Why does the variance at t use the return at t−1?
faq.answer: So that the volatility sitting on row t was knowable before r_t was. That is the RiskMetrics recursion. Putting r_t into var[t] would make any later Sharpe-style scaling use information from the return it is scaling.

faq.question: Is this GARCH?
faq.answer: No. GARCH(1,1) has a constant term and the two slopes are estimated. EWMA is the special case ω = 0 and α + β = 1, with λ chosen rather than fitted. It has no finite unconditional variance.
